scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that history shows human continuity, then argues its main benefit is the wider lessons it teaches; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: When we read about the past, we often notice how much people then resemble people now.
Some people argue that the main benefit of studying history is to dispel the illusion that we are very different from people who lived long ago.
I agree that history reveals how similar people have always been, but I believe this is only one of its benefits and not the main one.
First, history really does show how much human beings have stayed the same.
People in every age have loved, feared, hoped, and struggled in ways we easily recognise today.
For example, ancient letters and stories reveal jealousies and ambitions that feel strikingly modern.
This shows that studying the past can cure the proud illusion that we are entirely new and unique.
Realising this can make us humbler and more understanding toward people of other times.
It reminds us that today's problems are often old problems wearing new clothes.
To this extent, history truly does dispel the illusion of our difference.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why its main benefit is broader

sentences.text: Second, however, this is far from the main benefit that history offers.
The greatest value of history is that it helps us learn from the successes and mistakes of the past.
Consider how studying the causes of past wars can help leaders avoid repeating the same disasters.
Such lessons can shape wiser decisions and protect societies from old and dangerous errors.
History also explains how the present world came to be, from its borders to its beliefs.
It teaches how societies change over time, which is just as important as seeing how people stay the same.
These deeper benefits matter far more than simply correcting one illusion about ourselves.
In conclusion, history does usefully remind us that we are not so different from people of the past.
But its main benefit lies in the lessons and understanding it offers for the present and future.
We study history less to see ourselves in the past than to learn how to live more wisely now.
